title: 'What Do You Need?' Wednesday: An AI-infused Edition
author: Episcopal Academy CTL
summary: The Episcopal Academy Center for Teaching and Learning's weekly digest, The Beacon, curates and editorializes on four separate AI-and-education pieces under its recurring "What Do You Need?" format. The editors open with Dan Willingham's warning that students should only use AI for tasks they already know how to do well, adding their own quibble about how narrowly Willingham defines "AI use" given newer tools built for guided cognitive friction. They pair this with Cambridge professor Rupert Wegerif's argument that AI exposes a confusion between performance and education, reframing the goal of teaching as expanding "dialogic space" rather than producing polished output. The roundup closes with pointers to Teddy Svoronos and Francis Su modeling transparency about their own AI stances in the classroom, and to David Epstein's case for the enduring value of amateurism in a fast-changing technological moment. Each linked item comes with the CTL's own practical classroom prompt, making the digest as much a curated teaching toolkit as a reading list.
points: Curates and editorializes on four distinct AI-in-education pieces (Willingham, Wegerif, Svoronos/Su, Epstein) rather than simply linking them, adding the CTL's own classroom-ready prompts to each.
Pushes back on Dan Willingham's framing that AI use means only engaging an unguarded chatbot, arguing newer tools built for guided cognitive friction complicate that simple binary.
Highlights Rupert Wegerif's reframing of AI's classroom disruption as an opportunity to recover 'the expansion of dialogic space' as education's actual goal, rather than mere performance.
Closes with David Epstein's argument (from his book Range) for the enduring value of amateurism as a stabilizing disposition during rapid technological change.
quotes: We are big fans of anything Dan Willingham writes, so we're kicking off this week's WDYN with his recent warning on AI use in educational settings. Arguing that students should only use AI to do things they know how to do well, we can't disagree with many of the underlying, cognitive principles Dan points towards.

By making this confusion between performance and education so clearly visible, AI offers us a great opportunity to rethink what we are doing in education. It is to recover what is most educational about education: the expansion of dialogic space.
Try this: For your next writing assignment, name explicitly which parts students must produce unaided, and tell them why those parts are the point.
Teddy Svoronos and Francis Su share the ways they're tweaking their teaching and sharing their concerns and hopes with students in the classroom this year.
Leaning on his research from the book Range, Epstein gives credence to the value of amateurism amidst these turbulent times.
